analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare and Medicaid drug plans to pay pharmacies their acquisition costs and pass rebates to patients.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced December 11, 2025 with 41 cosponsors split between both parties and was referred to two House committees, where it has not yet received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the rules for how pharmacies get paid under Medicare Part D and Medicaid. It would force insurers and the middlemen that run their drug benefits, called pharmacy benefit managers, to reimburse in-network pharmacies at the drug's actual national average acquisition cost plus a small fee, to apply manufacturer rebates to patients' copays at the pharmacy counter, and to stop steering patients to pharmacies the middlemen own. It adds annual compliance certifications, criminal penalties of up to $1 million and 10 years in prison, civil fines up to $1 million per violation, and new public reporting of drug acquisition prices in Medicaid [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid enrollees, who would see manufacturer rebates applied directly to their copays at the pharmacy counter instead of being absorbed upstream, and independent and community pharmacies, which would be guaranteed payment at their actual acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee and would gain protection from being pushed out of networks in favor of pharmacies owned by the benefit managers themselves [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare Part D plans and Medicaid managed-care contracts to reimburse in-network pharmacies the national average drug acquisition cost plus the lesser of 4% or $50, plus a dispensing fee matching the state Medicaid rate, and bars any fee that claws those payments back [S2].
Requires manufacturer rebates to be applied at the point of sale to reduce a patient's copay or coinsurance, rather than being retained downstream [S2].

Prohibits steering, broadly defined to include preferred and narrow pharmacy networks, differential cost-sharing that punishes patients for using non-affiliated pharmacies, and accreditation or delivery rules that exclude in-network pharmacies [S2].

Creates criminal penalties of up to a $1,000,000 fine, 10 years in prison, or both for a pharmacy benefits manager that knowingly and willfully fails the payment or rebate rules or engages in steering, plus civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000,000 per act [S2].
Expands Medicaid drug price surveys to all pharmacy types, requires pharmacies to report acquisition prices net of all price concessions, and requires the Secretary to make the results public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated mail-order and specialty pharmacies, which lose their current freedom to set pharmacy reimbursement below cost, steer volume to their own stores, and keep rebate spreads. Medicare plans and Medicaid managed-care entities take on compliance and certification duties, and some of the higher pharmacy reimbursement could flow into plan costs [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies

drawbacks.text: Pegging pharmacy reimbursement to a fixed national average cost plus a capped fee may not reflect what every pharmacy actually pays, and dispensing fees set at state Medicaid rates are low in many states, so some pharmacies could still be underpaid [S2].

Higher guaranteed pharmacy reimbursement and point-of-sale rebates could raise plan costs, which eventually show up in Medicare premiums, Medicaid financing, and taxpayer subsidies, though the bill requires plans to account for rebate remittances in their bids to limit that effect [S2].

The steering ban is written broadly, prohibiting preferred pharmacy networks and differential cost-sharing entirely, which eliminates plan-design tools that can direct patients to lower-cost mail-order channels [S2].

The criminal penalty of up to 10 years in prison applies to knowingly and willfully failing a complex set of payment and rebate rules, a sweeping sanction that critics would call disproportionate for billing disputes [S2].

Requiring every pharmacy, including mail-order, specialty, and clinic pharmacies, to respond to acquisition-price surveys and report net costs adds administrative burden, and the bill excludes charitable and nonprofit pharmacies from the survey [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and well targeted: patients get rebates at the counter instead of losing them in the middle of the supply chain, and the pharmacies people actually use get paid what the drugs cost. The main cost, higher plan spending, is partially blunted by forcing plans to subtract rebate remittances from their bids. The biggest design risks are the one-size-fits-all reimbursement formula and the breadth of the steering ban and criminal penalties, which a careful committee process would likely need to refine. As written, the upside for patients and small pharmacies outweighs the downside, but the rough edges are real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 11, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, where it now sits with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled [S4].

narrative.text: Representative Jake Auchincloss introduced the bill on December 11, 2025, with 21 original cosponsors listed in the introduction, 12 of them Republicans [S2].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, in each case for consideration of provisions within their jurisdiction [S4].
As of the latest action history, 41 members had cosponsored the bill, 25 Republicans and 16 Democrats [S3].
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has been reached yet. For now, pharmacy benefit managers' existing practices continue unchanged while the bill waits in committee, so the status quo serves them. Whether patients and pharmacies come out ahead depends on whether the bill ever gets a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support so far is bipartisan: of 41 cosponsors, 25 are Republicans and 16 are Democrats, and the original introduction included 12 Republicans alongside the Democratic sponsor; no votes have occurred to test the split.

industries.note: The bill strikes at the core of the PBM business model: it requires paying pharmacies at cost plus a capped fee, remitting rebates to plans and patients, and bans steering patients to PBM-affiliated pharmacies, with felony-level penalties for knowing violations. For ordinary people, PBMs' margin currently sits between their copays and what their pharmacy gets paid.

Community pharmacies are often reimbursed below their acquisition cost under PBM contracts. A guaranteed cost-plus payment and a bar on excluding them from networks directly addresses the financial pressure closing rural and neighborhood drugstores.

These affiliated pharmacies rely on plans steering patients their way. The bill's steering definition outlaws preferred and narrow networks, differential cost-sharing, and accreditation tricks that route volume to affiliates.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicaid managed-care plans
industries.note: Plans must write PBM contracts with these guarantees, certify compliance, and pass rebates to patients, but the bill also requires rebate remittances to be subtracted from plan bids, so plan financing adjusts rather than purely rising. The main cost is compliance and loss of flexible network design.

analysis.trajectory: With bipartisan backing but referral to two committees, the bill's fate depends entirely on whether either committee schedules it. Most bills at this stage die without a vote, but PBM reform has unusual cross-party attention this Congress, so a hearing or the absorption of its provisions into a larger health or drug-pricing package is the more plausible path than standalone passage. Without leadership scheduling action, it is likely to stall in committee.
